enrichment.short_title: Administrative Court guidance on section 55 asylum support interim relief
key_facts: Multiple judicial review applications concerning section 55 asylum support were listed before Maurice Kay J for permission and interim relief in October 2003.
Asylum support cases had grown to about a quarter of Administrative Court lodgements and roughly 800 active cases, with over 90% of interim relief applications succeeding.
The Secretary of State did not oppose permission or interim relief in the seven remaining cases, and the court issued procedural guidance to reduce avoidable litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review applications for permission and interim relief, with submissions on court-wide guidance for section 55 asylum support cases.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted and interim relief continued in the listed cases; the court issued detailed guidance on handling section 55 and Article 3 applications.
enrichment.ratio: Where asylum support is withdrawn after an adverse section 55 decision, the Secretary of State should establish an efficient Article 3 decision-making procedure and normally continue interim support without a court order when judicial review is indicated; claimants should avoid premature and out-of-hours applications, and the court will generally deal with interim relief on paper without abridging time for acknowledgment of service.
legal_issues: How the Administrative Court should manage the volume of section 55 asylum support cases
Whether the Secretary of State has power to provide emergency accommodation pending judicial review
The proper approach to interim relief where Article 3 is arguable
Whether claimants' solicitors were improperly using public funding

notes: Full Divisional Court judgment on roadside breath test procedure and PACE s78.

enrichment.short_title: Roadside breath test mouthpiece reuse did not invalidate conviction
key_facts: The defendant was stopped after a positive roadside breath test on a Lion Alcometer SL400A and later provided positive samples at the police station.
The magistrates found the roadside test invalid because the officer did not change the mouthpiece between failed and successful attempts, and excluded all breath evidence under section 78 PACE.
The Divisional Court held the manufacturer's instructions did not require a fresh mouthpiece after an incomplete first attempt by the same suspect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a drink-driving charge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the magistrates' court with a direction to convict.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to change a roadside breath-test mouthpiece after an incomplete first attempt by the same suspect does not mean the device was incorrectly assembled or invalidate the test; and simple maladministration of a roadside breath test, without more, is insufficient to exclude properly obtained police station breath evidence under section 78 PACE following the change in law reflected in R v Fox.
legal_issues: Whether a fresh mouthpiece must be used for each roadside breath test attempt on an Alcometer SL400A
Whether an improperly administered roadside test invalidates arrest under section 6(5) Road Traffic Act 1988
The proper exercise of discretion under section 78 PACE to exclude police station breath specimens

enrichment.short_title: MHRT medical member employed by detaining Trust not biased
key_facts: The claimant was detained under section 3 at Rathbone Hospital, run by Mersey Care NHS Trust.
Dr Ahmed Izmeth, a consultant psychiatrist employed by Mersey Care but working in a separate geographical directorate, sat as the medical member when the tribunal refused discharge.
The claimant argued there was a real possibility of subconscious bias because the medical member's employer was a party to the proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review to quash a Mental Health Review Tribunal refusal to discharge, following permission granted by Gibbs J.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the tribunal's decision was compatible with Article 6 and the common law test for bias.
enrichment.ratio: A fair-minded and informed observer would not conclude there was a real possibility of bias where a medical tribunal member employed by the detaining NHS Trust had no connection with the patient's hospital, no prior dealings with the patient or witnesses, was subject to professional and protocol safeguards, and could not be disciplined for tribunal decisions.
legal_issues: Whether a medical member employed by the detaining NHS Trust can sit without breaching Article 6 or the Porter/Lawal bias test
The meaning of 'officer' in Rule 8(2)(b) of the Mental Health Review Tribunal Rules 1983
Whether consequences of excluding such members from tribunals are relevant to the bias inquiry

enrichment.short_title: Sri Lankan asylum appeal dismissed despite notice dispute
key_facts: A Sri Lankan national's asylum and human rights appeal was determined on the papers under Rule 43 after he and his solicitor did not attend the hearing.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal, finding notice had been served but also that the appeal had no reasonable prospect of success on the merits.
The claimant argued the IAT had been Wednesbury unreasonable in rejecting his solicitor's assertion that no notice was received, relying on R (Karagoz) v IAT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review dismissed; although the IAT's treatment of the notice issue was Wednesbury unreasonable, the claim had no real prospect of success on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator properly proceeds under Rule 43 after satisfying herself that notice was sent, a tribunal may still err by failing to weigh a professional assertion of non-receipt; however, leave should be refused if, on the objective country evidence for Sri Lankan Tamils after Jeyachandran, the appellant could not show an exceptional case with any real prospect of success.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in proceeding under Rule 43 without a hearing
Whether the IAT was Wednesbury unreasonable in rejecting assertions that notice was not received
Whether procedural unfairness entitled the claimant to relief where the substantive appeal had no prospect of success

enrichment.short_title: Home Office pathologist removed after audit non-cooperation
key_facts: Dr Lannas, a Home Office registered forensic pathologist, failed to respond to audit requests for autopsy reports after adverse publicity and an inconclusive disciplinary inquiry.
Dr Rothwell wrote personally offering flexibility on audit material, but her solicitor's reply was held to shut the door on cooperation rather than seek a way forward.
The Policy Advisory Board for Forensic Pathology, with ministerial approval, removed her from the register for non-compliance with audit requirements.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim to quash removal from the Home Office Register of Pathologists.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a registered forensic pathologist fails to submit work for audit despite clear obligations and a personal invitation to cooperate flexibly, removal from the Home Office register is a lawful exercise of the Board's discretion and does not require a further hearing or await General Medical Council outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors may charge estate administration by time and value
key_facts: Kippax Beaumont Lewis administered Sir Geoffrey Hulton's estate worth nearly £10 million and billed both on time (£386,459) and on estate value (£227,689 plus VAT).
Costs Judge Rogers held solicitors could not charge both an hourly rate and a separate percentage of estate value.
The residuary beneficiary's assignee appealed on preliminary issues as to value-based charges, regressive scales, and hourly rates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Costs Judge Rogers' decision on preliminary issues in detailed assessment of estate administration costs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; matter remitted to the costs judge to assess fair and reasonable remuneration in light of the court's guidance.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors administering an estate may, absent prior agreement, charge both by reference to time and by a separate value element provided value is not counted twice, the overall charge remains fair and reasonable under the 1994 Order, and high-value estates should usually use a regressive percentage scale informed by authorities such as Maltby v D J Freeman.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court wrongly adjourned trial for absent witnesses
key_facts: A 15-year-old defendant faced trial for assault occasioning actual bodily harm before Balham Youth Court.
On two listing dates the prosecution witnesses failed to attend; on the second occasion they claimed to think the trial was 'tomorrow or the next day', later explaining they had forgotten.
The district judge granted a further adjournment with reluctance, despite the defendant attending on time and the CPS having properly warned witnesses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the youth court's decision granting a prosecution adjournment.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; order adjourning the trial quashed, with the inevitable consequence that the case would have been dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Applications to adjourn criminal trials for non-attendance of prosecution witnesses must be rigorously scrutinised; where witnesses have been properly warned, no intimidation is shown, and the explanation for absence is not credible, especially in the Youth Court where expedition matters, refusal of adjournment and dismissal is appropriate.
legal_issues: The proper exercise of discretion to adjourn when prosecution witnesses fail to attend
Whether the youth court's acceptance of the witnesses' explanation was irrational
The balance between expedition and fairness in Youth Court proceedings

enrichment.short_title: Insurance amendment allowed despite contractual one-year time bar
key_facts: British Credit Trust claimed under a motor hire-purchase indemnity policy for losses arising as agreements terminated after issue of the claim form.
The insurer resisted amendment to add post-issue claims, arguing a contractual one-year time bar in policy clause 5(n) and abandonment of declaratory relief pleaded in the claim form.
The claim form sought a declaration of liability for further amounts due under the policy, but the original particulars omitted that declaratory relief through oversight.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to amend particulars of claim at a case management hearing following adjournment by Toulson J.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend granted with the amendment relating back to the date of the claim form; no abandonment or effective time-bar precluded the amendment.
enrichment.ratio: A claim for declaratory relief in the claim form can stop time running under a contractual one-year action clause in an insurance policy; omission of that relief from particulars does not abandon it, and the court may permit amendment relating back unless the insurer would lose a genuine contractual time-bar defence.
legal_issues: Whether declaratory relief pleaded in the claim form but omitted from particulars was abandoned
The proper construction of the policy's one-year contractual time bar in clause 5(n)

Whether amendment may relate back to defeat a contractual limitation period

enrichment.short_title: Revenue not bound by General Commissioners' roll-over relief findings
key_facts: Mr Barnett sold 14 Belsize Park Gardens in April 1986 and sought roll-over relief by reinvesting in 13 Elrington Road, Hackney, but the unconditional contract was not entered until July 1989.
The General Commissioners found he had a firm intention to reinvest within time but was prevented by planning disputes, yet held they had no jurisdiction over the Board's section 152(3) discretion.

The Inland Revenue refused to extend the three-year reinvestment period, finding no circumstances beyond Mr Barnett's control and that he pursued the Hackney property because of links to the vendor Foldell Ltd.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Board of Inland Revenue's refusal to exercise discretion under section 152(3) TCGA 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: The discretion to extend the roll-over reinvestment period under section 152(3) is vested exclusively in the Board of Inland Revenue, and General Commissioners cannot make findings that bind the Board's exercise of that discretion; CG60640 indicates when extension is permitted but does not convert factual findings before the commissioners into a mandatory exercise of discretion.
legal_issues: Whether General Commissioners' factual findings on section 152(3) discretion bind the Inland Revenue
The relationship between CG60640 and section 152(3)
Whether planning delay and vendor links amounted to circumstances beyond the taxpayer's control

enrichment.short_title: No Community law damages claim against state aid recipient

statutes_considered.title: Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community (Treaty of Paris)

key_facts: Betws Anthracite, a Welsh colliery, sued Preussag Anthrazit for about £4.5 million loss allegedly caused by misuse of German state aid in 1996-97.
The European Commission decision of 29 July 1998 found Preussag misused DEM 9.8 million and DEM 6.8 million of coal aid, distorting competition in the UK sized-anthracite market.
Preussag argued Betws had no private law cause of action against the aid recipient and that any loss was not causally proved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial claim for damages following a Commission state aid decision, tried with full evidence on liability and quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Betws had no viable Community law cause of action against Preussag, and causation was not established.
enrichment.ratio: Following SFEI, a competitor has no Community law tort against the recipient of unlawful state aid for misuse of aid; the Commission decision was addressed to Germany and at best supported a claim against the Member State, not Preussag, and Betws failed to prove that the identified misuse of aid was an effective cause of its losses.
legal_issues: Whether a competitor may sue the recipient of unlawful ECSC/EC state aid for damages in the national courts
The evidential effect of a Commission state aid decision against a competitor's claim
Whether Preussag's price cuts were caused by misuse of aid rather than commercial price competition
Quantum of loss if liability had been established
